title: Harmful speech
hook: speech that harms, even when it's true

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was achrayut, and your line was carry your share. What did you claim as yours? Today a new stretch begins, on speech, and it starts with the tongue. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

Did you hear about Dan? He got let go. Apparently he'd been missing deadlines for months. Two people at a coffee machine. Every word is true. Nobody is lying, nobody is shouting, and nobody would call it cruel. It's just news, passed along with a little lift in the voice. Dan isn't there. He'll never know this conversation happened. And yet Jewish tradition has a name for that sentence, and it treats it as a serious wrong. Today's word is the name.
screen: `EVERY WORD IS TRUE.` → `DAN ISN'T THERE.` → `THE SENTENCE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Lashon hara. Literally, the evil tongue: speech that harms, even when it's true. Turn it four ways. First, the true part. Saying something false about a person is a different wrong, and it gets its own name later this week. Lashon hara is about true things: a failure, a weakness, an embarrassing story, told about someone in a way that lowers them. Being accurate doesn't make it kind. Second, the story the tradition points to. In the book of Numbers, Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses. God's anger burns, and Miriam is struck with a skin disease and shut outside the camp for seven days, while the whole people waits for her. Deuteronomy later tells Israel to remember what God did to Miriam on the way out of Egypt, and tradition reads that remembering as a warning about speech. Third, the three it wounds. The Talmud, in tractate Arakhin, says lashon hara kills three people: the one who speaks it, the one who hears it, and the one it's about. The one who speaks gets smaller. The one who hears can't unhear it. And the one it's about pays for a conversation they weren't in. Fourth, the exception. The tradition does allow some harmful truth to be spoken, when it's needed to protect someone, like warning a friend about a business partner who cheats. The rules for that are careful, and the purpose has to be help, not entertainment. That's the line: does this sentence protect someone, or does it just make a good story?
screen: `TRUE, AND STILL HARMFUL.` · `REMEMBER WHAT GOD DID TO MIRIAM.` · `IT KILLS THREE.` · `PROTECTION, NOT ENTERTAINMENT.` · then, large: `NO GOSSIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare for a day without gossip. Settle, and breathe. Think of where gossip usually finds you. A group chat. A lunch table. A phone call with one particular friend. A family dinner. Picture the moment when someone's name comes up and the story starts to lean. Now find your sentence for that moment, something easy to say: I don't really know the whole story. Or: let's talk about something else. Or just a change of subject. Practice it once in your head. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Lashon hara. The evil tongue: true words about someone that lower them, when no one needs protecting. Today's word.
Your line: no gossip. Today, for one full day, say nothing about anyone who isn't there that you wouldn't say if they were standing beside you. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the laws of guarding speech a little each day, and some communities and schools hold days or hours set aside for speaking no lashon hara at all.

fork.setup: Miriam has spoken against Moses, and she is shut outside the camp. the people are ready to travel. what do they do?
options: move on and let her catch up.
wait, and not travel until she is brought back in.
fork.reveal: Numbers says the people did not journey until Miriam was brought in again. the whole camp waited on one sentence spoken against a brother.

original.note: Hebrew: the evil tongue; harmful speech about another person.

trapdoor: what you thought: lashon hara means lying about people.
what it means: true speech that lowers someone, spoken when no one needs protecting.
what a scholar hears: Miriam in Numbers 12, remembered in Deuteronomy 24:9; Arakhin 15b, it kills three; and the careful rules for speech that protects.

notes: Editor pass: 'the rabbis read' changed to 'tradition reads' for the Deuteronomy 24:9 reading, which the cited verse does not state.
Numbers 12: 'seven days' outside the camp and the people waiting are stated in the text (12:14–15); confirm 'skin disease' as rendering of tzara'at.
Deuteronomy 24:9 paraphrased; the rabbinic reading of it as a warning about speech is attributed to 'the rabbis'.
Arakhin 15b: lashon hara 'kills three' paraphrased; confirm citation.
The protective exception (to'elet) is described generally; the detailed conditions come from later codes (the Chafetz Chaim, tomorrow). Confirm wording.
Teach says false speech 'gets its own name later this week' (motzi shem ra, day 1272).
